case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbour Leisure Tours (HLT) is a private limited company in the tourism and leisure sector, operating whale-watching and harbour cruises from a coastal marina and employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Marais, HLT runs a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, so skippers and crew help shape sailing schedules. It plans to invest $420,000 in a new catamaran and an online booking platform, financed by a $250,000 ten-year bank loan and $170,000 retained profit. HLT has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and currently produces 22,000 units a year, each unit being one passenger cruise. Recently labour turnover has reached 14% and complaints about boarding delays have grown, threatening the reputation Sofia built.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Customer and Operations Extract — Q3 2025: HLT sold 5,600 cruise tickets last quarter at an average price of $28.00, with 94% of departures running on time. Boarding complaints fell from 46 to 19 per month after a new queue system. Safety checks found 2.1% of life jackets failing inspection, down from 3.4% a year earlier. A survey of 500 tourists found 68% would book again if online booking were offered and 57% chose HLT for its eco-credentials. Retraining each crew member in customer care costs $480 at the local maritime college.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for HLT's $250,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, raising the crew wage bill. (3) Marine fuel and insurance input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year while tourism inflation is 6.3%, and inbound visitor arrivals grew 4.2%.

questions.question_text: HLT plans to fund part of its new catamaran with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HLT of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $170,000 of retained profit costs HLT no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the company already carries fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $250,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid as interest can be spent on crew training at $480 per person to tackle the 14% labour turnover, or on marketing the $28.00 cruises, keeping more of the $12.00 earned on each passenger unit.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the $420,000 catamaran and booking platform cannot be seized if visitor numbers disappoint. Sofia Marais also keeps full ownership and control of the flat structure and democratic leadership she built, because no lender can impose conditions on sailing schedules or on how the new online platform is run. With 38 staff depending on the business, avoiding extra debt commitments makes the expansion safer and steadier. Even allowing for the roughly $1,875 a year that the 0.75-point rise to 5.0% would add on a variable-rate $250,000 loan, the retained-profit route keeps more of the $12.00 contribution inside HLT to reinvest in the 22,000-unit cruise operation and in the $480 crew retraining that should ease the 14% turnover.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HLT, its loan, its retained profit and its tourism operations.

questions.question_text: HLT is promoting its new cruise schedule. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HLT choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A national TV campaign would build awareness of whale-watching cruises quickly across the whole country and could attract tourists who have never heard of HLT. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a private limited company with only 38 staff and a $420,000 expansion already funded by debt, and much of the audience lives far from the coastal marina and cannot book a $28.00 trip, so spend wastage would be high.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper and reaches precisely the coastal catchment and day-trippers who can visit the marina, and it suits urgent messages about the new catamaran schedule. Its weakness is narrow reach: the survey of 500 tourists showed demand from visitors beyond the immediate area, and radio cannot reach them, limiting ticket sales growth.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and lifestyle influencers can target the 68% of surveyed tourists who said they would rebook with online booking and the 57% drawn by eco-credentials, with measurable engagement at low cost and national reach. Results build more slowly than television, but the content can showcase the whale-watching experience directly.

Recommendation: HLT should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact segments in the research, costs far less than television and reaches further than local radio, and it drives the online booking platform. Television is rejected as unaffordable and wasteful; radio is rejected as too local; influencers are the best fit for a 38-staff operator. Reinvesting the marketing saving in the $480 crew training would also help cut the 14% turnover that forces repeated recruitment, so the campaign and the training budget can be planned together. Low-cost digital promotion leaves more cash to honour the eco-credentials that 57% of tourists value.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HLT with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HLT with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: HLT's labour turnover has reached 14%. Explain two benefits for HLT of using democratic leadership to improve staff motivation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 38 employees a real voice in how the new catamaran and sailing rota are organised, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Skippers and crew who help shape schedules are more likely to feel valued and stay, directly reducing the 14% labour turnover and the $480-per-person retraining bill, while protecting the smooth flat structure Sofia Marais established.

Point 2: Consulting the crew generates practical ideas from the people handling boarding and safety checks every day, so complaints about boarding delays can be solved faster and the 2.1% life-jacket defect rate pushed down further. Involvement builds commitment to HLT's reputation for whale-watching cruises, which supports the 5,600 tickets sold last quarter and the 94% on-time departure record, keeping the $28.00 service reliable while the new booking platform beds in. The $480-per-person training cost is an investment in retention as well as service quality, and with a workforce of 38 the saving from fewer leavers quickly outweighs it. Listening to skippers also makes the democratic structure genuine rather than nominal, strengthening commitment to Sofia Marais's business.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HLT's labour turnover, training cost and service quality.

questions.question_text: HLT must train crew in customer care. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local maritime college. Which should HLT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching crew on the actual catamaran and boarding process is directly relevant to HLT's own operations, costs no course fees and keeps staff productive while they learn, protecting the 94% on-time departure record and the effort behind falling boarding complaints. The drawback is that trainers are working skippers whose own duties suffer, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no formal certificate for the 14% of staff most likely to leave.

Off-the-job training: The local maritime college course at $480 per crew member gives structured customer-care skills and a recognised qualification, which could raise service standards and help retain the 38 staff. However, it removes crew from the marina, cutting short-term capacity during the launch, and the generic content may not match HLT's exact boarding routines, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: HLT should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, backed by short college sessions for senior skippers. It is cheaper, specific to HLT's catamaran and avoids losing capacity while labour turnover is 14%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because sending many crew away at once would disrupt sailings and cost fees on top of the $420,000 expansion; college modules can be added later once the new schedule is stable. Complaints have already fallen from 46 to 19 a month, and protecting that trend matters more than a certificate alone. On-the-job coaching keeps the 38 staff productive, while a short college module later can add formal recognition without losing sailings or adding to the $420,000 bill.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HLT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of HLT.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of HLT with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HLT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($28.00 − $16.00) = $180,000 ÷ $12.00 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 passenger cruise units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $28.00 − $16.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HLT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 15,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 22,000 units to confirm the cruise business is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 7,000 units before the new catamaran is needed.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 lets HLT test a discount on the $28.00 ticket price; for example, a $2.00 cut leaves $10.00 contribution, so managers can judge whether extra bookings would still cover the $180,000 fixed costs.
3. The break-even target helps Sofia Marais plan repayments on the $250,000 loan for the $420,000 expansion, checking that 22,000 passenger units generate enough contribution before further borrowing.
4. Average total cost of $24.18 a unit ($180,000 ÷ 22,000 + $16.00) can be benchmarked each quarter against the 2.1% life-jacket defect rate and 14% labour turnover to target waste and training needs as fuel and insurance costs rise 9.6%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 22,000-unit output; ticket-price discount modelling against $180,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $420,000 expansion; and average total cost benchmarking at $24.18 to tackle defects and turnover.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HLT's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HLT's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.95 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $50,000 + $110,000 + $55,000 = $215,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $180,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.50 and 2025 = $215,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.95. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($180,000 − $60,000) ÷ $120,000 = 1.00 and 2025 = ($215,000 − $50,000) ÷ $110,000 = 1.50.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. The 2024 figure of 1.50 rose to 1.95, meaning current assets cover short-term debts more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $120,000 to $110,000 while cash rose from $30,000 to $55,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, improved from 1.00 to 1.50, so HLT no longer depends on selling stock to pay debts — important while it services a $250,000 loan and funds a $420,000 expansion. However, trade receivables rose from $90,000 to $110,000, tying up cash; if tour operators pay late, the stronger position could weaken quickly.

Conclusion: HLT's financial position has improved. Both measures rose (1.50 to 1.95 and 1.00 to 1.50) and the improvement does not rely on inventories. The residual risk is rising receivables, so HLT should tighten credit control while proceeding with the catamaran investment. The $55,000 cash balance also gives HLT room to absorb the 9.6% fuel and insurance rise noted in the bulletin, which a more stretched position could not. Credit control on the $110,000 of receivables remains the priority so that the improvement is sustained into the next trading year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether HLT's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HLT of introducing eco-friendly cruise practices.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-friendly practices such as waste reduction and cleaner fuelling reinforce the 57% of surveyed tourists who chose HLT for its eco-credentials, supporting the $28.00 ticket price and the 68% who would rebook through the new online platform. With marine fuel and insurance input costs up 9.6%, efficiency measures can also trim the $16.00 variable cost per unit, protecting the $12.00 contribution while attracting the 4.2% growth in visitor arrivals.

Disadvantage: Greener equipment and certification carry upfront costs that would add to fixed costs of $180,000 a year at a time when HLT already services a $250,000 loan and is spending $420,000 on a catamaran. If the investment cannot be passed on through higher prices, the 38-staff operator's margins narrow; and if eco-claims are not delivered, the reputation Sofia Marais built and the 57% eco-conscious segment could be lost. If the eco-credentials claim is not backed by real action, the 57% who chose HLT for that reason could be lost, so the investment must be genuine. Managers can measure progress through the 2.1% defect rate and the 19 monthly complaints already tracked.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HLT's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in fuel and insurance costs will affect HLT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If HLT's $250,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $250,000 = $1,875 a year. That is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may still deter tourists and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $420,000 catamaran, but HLT can cap this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 per hour): With a workforce of 38, most crew and boarding roles are hourly-paid, so this feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the sound judgement is to compare with the given output of 22,000 passenger units across 38 staff, about 579 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable from the $12.00 contribution; if labour turnover of 14% persists, unit labour cost rises.

Fuel and insurance inflation (9.6%): The $16.00 variable cost per unit is where fuel and insurance sit, but the insert never breaks it down, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $16.00 rose 9.6%, that is 0.096 × $16.00 = $1.54 per unit, and at 22,000 units about $33,880 a year. Even a smaller $1.00-per-unit rise costs $22,000 a year, cutting contribution from $12.00 toward $11.00.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in fuel and insurance will have the greatest impact, because it recurs on every one of the 22,000 units and directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $420,000 expansion. The wage rise is significant but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $1,875.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HLT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HLT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HLT with a well-justified judgment that fuel and insurance inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
